events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Arjun proposes Arjun, Sam. As leader for Mission 1, I'm proposing myself and Sam for a balanced two-player team. This keeps the opening simple and gives the table a clear, fair starting point for discussion.
I’d prefer Elena and Sam for the opening mission: I can only be certain of my own alignment, and we have no public evidence yet about anyone else. Arjun, what led you to choose Sam specifically?

Elena, fair question. I chose Sam because he hasn't been part of any suspicion yet, and a two-player team with me on it keeps the opening small while giving us a clean read on the outcome. I'm also taking responsibility as leader for the choice. I'm open to your alternative of Elena and Sam, and I think the table should weigh that against keeping the team I proposed before we vote.

Arjun, your explanation for choosing Sam doesn't give us much reason to trust either member of the proposed team. I'd prefer Elena and Sam, since I know my own alignment. Sam, would you support that alternative?

Elena, I appreciate the question. From my seat, both proposed pairings are one known-good member—me—plus one player I cannot verify. I do not have public evidence that makes Arjun more or less trustworthy than you, and I don't think the first mission should hinge on speculation. Arjun's proposal includes me, so I can guarantee at least one Success card from my side; I am willing to vote for Arjun and Sam. If the table prefers Elena and Sam, I would consider it, but I don't see a reason to overturn the leader's current team based solely on the opening discussion.

I’m not persuaded that Arjun and Sam is the best opening team. Sam’s willingness to support it is understandable from his perspective, but it doesn’t establish Arjun’s alignment. I still prefer Elena and Sam and would vote against the current proposal.

Elena, I agree that none of us can verify anyone else's alignment yet, and that includes me. That is why I'm not asking the table to trust me. Mission 1 is only a two-player team, so the choice is small, and the proposal should be judged on that. I chose Sam because he has not been part of any suspicion, and Sam has already stated why he supports this team. Changing the team now would not add evidence about anyone. I'd suggest we vote on the current proposal and let the mission result give us real information.

I think Arjun's proposal is reasonable for Mission 1. He's taken responsibility as leader and has a clear rationale — Sam is not under suspicion, and the team is simple and transparent. Elena, you've been pushing hard for a team that includes you instead of Arjun, and I have to ask why you're so insistent on being on this mission yourself. You say it's because you can only trust your own alignment, but that logic applies equally to every player at this table. If anything, a player who is very vocal about wanting to be on the team — rather than being willing to trust others — is worth watching. Arjun has given a straightforward explanation, Sam has endorsed it, and I don't see a strong reason to overturn the leader's choice. I'd support the current team of Arjun and Sam.

I want to reinforce what I said before. Arjun's proposal of Arjun and Sam is straightforward and transparent for Mission 1. Elena has been consistently pushing for a team that includes herself, and I think we should pay attention to that pattern. The two-player team is small, and either pairing gives us limited information — but Arjun as leader has given his reasoning, Sam has endorsed the team, and there's no concrete reason to overturn it. Elena, your insistence on being on the team yourself rather than supporting the leader's choice is the only real point of contention here, and it doesn't benefit the group. I'd rather we approve Arjun and Sam, run the mission, and use the actual result to guide our next steps instead of speculating about motives.

I haven't weighed in yet, so I want to put my perspective out there. Arjun proposing himself and Sam is standard procedure for the first proposal of Mission 1. Elena, your logic that you only know your own alignment applies to all of us, but substituting yourself for Arjun doesn't make the team any more verifiable from my seat. At the same time, Leo, I wouldn't read too deeply into Elena wanting to be on the team—Good players frequently argue that way early on when they have no other information. Since we have zero public evidence at this stage, Arjun's proposal is reasonable and gives us a baseline. I'm inclined to approve Arjun and Sam so we can get actual mission data.

I'm still backing Arjun and Sam as the Mission 1 team. Two players is the smallest option, and it gives us a clean result to learn from. Elena has pushed for her own inclusion in several messages, but she hasn't offered any evidence that Elena and Sam would be safer than the current team. I'd like the table to vote on the proposal as it stands so the mission result can guide us.

I want to reaffirm my support for Arjun and Sam as the Mission 1 team. We've had a thorough discussion, and the case for approving this proposal remains strong. Arjun has been transparent about his reasoning, Sam has endorsed it, and neither Omar nor I see a compelling reason to switch. Elena, your continued push for Elena and Sam without offering any concrete advantage over the current team is starting to look like a pattern worth noting — you're the only player consistently arguing against the leader's proposal. That said, the table seems aligned: Arjun, Sam, Leo, and Omar all support the current team. I'd like us to move forward and vote so we can get real mission data instead of more debate. Let's approve Arjun and Sam.
Arjun confirms Arjun, Sam. I'm keeping Arjun and Sam. Four players have spoken in favor of it, and the mission result will give us real information instead of more speculation about motives.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).
Elena proposes Elena, Sam, Omar. I’m including myself, Sam, and Omar. Mission 1 succeeded with Sam, though that alone does not prove alignment; this team also gives Omar a chance to participate.

Elena's proposal of Elena, Sam, Omar looks reasonable for Mission 2. Sam played on Mission 1 that succeeded, Omar hasn't been on a team yet so it's good to get him involved, and Elena as leader including herself is fair after she was shut out of Mission 1. The team gives us a mix of tested and untested players, which is exactly what we need after one success. I'd approve this team so we can move forward and gather more information from the result.

Elena's proposal of Elena, Sam, Omar is close, but I think there's a stronger option. Arjun was on Mission 1, which succeeded — he has a proven track record on a team, while Omar has no mission experience yet. Swapping Omar for Arjun gives us two players who've already been on a successful mission plus Elena as a fresh known-good leader. Omar will have plenty of opportunities on later missions. Elena, why not include Arjun given his successful Mission 1 record instead of putting Omar on before he's been tested?

Leo, a successful first mission is encouraging, but it doesn't prove either team member is Good: an Evil player can play Success. I chose Sam and Omar because Omar's first-mission comments seemed balanced, and Sam was on the successful team. I prefer keeping Elena, Sam, and Omar rather than treating Arjun's mission result as proof.

I support Elena's proposed team of Elena, Sam, and Omar. From my seat, I know I am Good and will submit a Success. Elena's caution regarding Mission 1 is entirely sound—a clean first mission does not guarantee both Arjun and Sam are Good, since an Evil player often plays Success on a two-person team. Bringing Sam forward while testing a new configuration is a sensible way to expand. I also noticed that Leo endorsed this exact proposal in his first remark, only to immediately backtrack and push for Arjun instead of me. Testing two members from Mission 1 together again would risk putting an undetected Evil player right back on the board. I think Elena's team is well-balanced, and I'm ready to vote to approve it.

I’m inclined to support Elena, Sam, Omar. Elena is the leader and included herself, Omar is untested and gives us new information, and I am on the team, so I can guarantee at least one Success from my seat. Mission 1’s clean result does not prove Arjun is Good, so replacing Omar with Arjun is not automatically stronger. Leo, you first said you would approve this exact team, then immediately argued to swap Omar for Arjun. Which team do you actually support, and why did your position change between those two statements?

Sam, fair challenge. My first remark was a broad endorsement of getting Omar involved, and when I actually thought about mission composition, I started second-guessing whether two Mission 1 members together again was the stronger read. I appreciate Omar and you both calling that out — you're right that it came across as inconsistent, and I don't want my waffling to distract from the real question: what team gives us the best information on Mission 2. Thinking it through, Elena's proposal of Elena, Sam, Omar actually does give us that. Sam's on a second mission, Omar gets tested for the first time, and Elena as leader is fresh. Omar's point about testing Arjun and Sam together again is well-taken — if one of them were hiding something, pairing them again could mask it. I'm going to support Elena, Sam, Omar as proposed. Elena, Omar, Sam — this team looks solid to me and I'd approve it.

I support Elena, Sam, and Omar for Mission 2. Mission 1 succeeded, but that doesn't tell us much about Omar or Elena. Elena has opposed every team that didn't include herself, starting with my proposal, and I'd like her to explain whether that reflects concern about the team or a wish for her own seat. Sam, you were on the Mission 1 team with me, so do you see anything in how Elena or Omar have behaved that worries you?

Arjun, I appreciate the direct question. I don’t have a concrete behavioral worry about Omar: his Mission 2 comments were measured, he correctly flagged Leo’s inconsistency, and he is untested, which makes his inclusion useful. Elena pushed hard against the Mission 1 team and wanted herself on it, but that is common early Good behavior and she has given a coherent reason: a clean Mission 1 doesn’t prove either member Good. As leader, including herself is normal. The proposed team of Elena, Sam, Omar keeps me on it, tests Omar for the first time, and does not re-run both Mission 1 members together. From my seat I know I will submit Success; I cannot verify Elena or Omar, so if this mission fails it would point at one of them. But I don’t see enough to reject it. Leo’s earlier flip from endorsing this team to pushing Arjun, then back, is the more notable inconsistency, but he has now stated he supports the proposal. I will vote to approve Elena, Sam, Omar and let the result give us information.

I'm inclined to approve Elena, Sam, and Omar, but I'm not comfortable with how much weight is being put on Mission 1. Mission 1 was a two-player success, and that tells us little about either player. Elena has pushed hard for her own inclusion since the first proposal, and she has made the argument about her own alignment in several messages. That's worth weighing, even if it isn't proof of anything. Omar, you argued that re-testing Arjun and Sam together could mask an Evil player. Do you think Elena being on this team is a meaningful check, given she has been the most insistent about her own seat? I'd like to hear your reasoning before I vote.

Arjun, to answer your question: I don't see Elena's push to be on teams as inherently suspicious. On Mission 1, advocating for yourself is standard behavior for Good players who have no reliable data on anyone else. On Mission 2, she is the leader, and leaders almost always include themselves. Is her presence a meaningful check? Yes, because it yields concrete information. From my perspective, I know I will submit Success. Sam has already completed one successful mission. If Elena is Good, this team should succeed cleanly and put Good at two wins. If a Fail card appears, knowing my own card limits the source strictly to Elena or Sam, which would also force us to re-evaluate Mission 1. Rejecting a leader's first proposal simply because she included herself isn't justified without hard evidence. This lineup tests both Elena and me while keeping Sam as a baseline. I'm satisfied with this composition and ready to approve.

I'm inclined to approve Elena, Sam, and Omar. Mission 1 succeeded, which is the only public data we have, and this team tests Omar without re-running the exact Mission 1 pair. Elena has pushed for her own seat across several messages, and I'd still like her to explain that pattern beyond a general preference for self-inclusion. That concern isn't enough to reject a leader's team on its own, so I'll vote approve and let Mission 2 give us real information.

I support Elena, Sam, and Omar for Mission 2. From my seat, I know I will submit Success, so this team gives the table at least one guaranteed Good card. Omar is untested and gets useful first-mission data, while Elena as leader including herself is normal and gives us a clean read on her leadership. Mission 1’s success does not prove Arjun or me Good, so I do not treat it as clearance for anyone. If this team fails, then from my perspective the source would be limited to Elena or Omar, which makes the result informative either way. I see no concrete reason to reject the proposal, and I will vote to approve Elena, Sam, and Omar.
Elena confirms Elena, Sam, Omar. I’m keeping Elena, Sam, and Omar. The discussion gives me no compelling reason to change the proposed lineup.
Team approved (5 approve, 0 reject).
Mission 2 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Omar proposes Omar, Sam. Missions 1 and 2 both succeeded cleanly, and Sam participated in both. Since I know I am Good, pairing myself with Sam creates the most reliable two-player team to secure our third win.

Omar's proposal of Omar and Sam is reasonable on the surface, but I think it leaves out a key player. Arjun has only been on Mission 1, while Sam has now been on both missions. We have far more information about Sam than about Arjun. Omar, why did you choose Sam over Arjun? I understand Sam has a successful track record, but a track record of two missions doesn't mean much when the fail threshold is one card — we need to test Arjun again to get a second data point on him. If Arjun were to play on this team and it succeeded, we'd have much stronger information than simply repeating Sam a third time. I'd prefer a team that includes Arjun alongside either Omar or Sam, so we're actively testing players who haven't been recently confirmed rather than coasting on someone who's already been on both missions. The whole point of Mission 3 should be to narrow down our uncertainty, and leaving Arjun off does the opposite of that.

Leo, your reasoning fundamentally misunderstands the board state. We are currently leading 2-0. The objective of Mission 3 is not to "narrow down uncertainty" or run experiments for future rounds—if this mission succeeds, Good wins the game on the spot. We do not need data for a Mission 4 that will never happen if we close it out now. Choosing Sam is the most logical choice: Sam has been on both successful missions with zero fail cards thrown. While it is theoretically possible an Evil player laid low twice, Sam is empirically our safest option. Swapping Sam for Arjun would increase our risk, not lower it, since Arjun has only been on one mission. Why are you pushing to gamble on an untested variable when we are one win away from victory?

Omar, I respect the push to close it out, but I think your logic about testing being irrelevant only holds if we're certain of the team. Sam has been on both missions — a third consecutive appearance adds no new data. Arjun has only been on Mission 1 and hasn't been retested since. At fail threshold 1, we can't afford to coast on two players who've both quietly been present on clean missions. I'd argue for Omar and Arjun: you know your own alignment, and Arjun gets his second test. If it succeeds, we close it out with two players we've both directly verified. If it fails, we immediately know where to look. Leaving Arjun off again just means we're betting everything on Sam's streak of two missions — that's not proof, it's a pattern that a single Evil player could easily maintain across two rounds at this threshold. Omar, if you're confident in your own role, why not pair yourself with the one player who hasn't been tested since Mission 1 instead of rotating Sam for a third straight run? That gives us real coverage on Arjun while keeping you on the team to anchor it.

Leo, your argument that we should risk failing Mission 3 just so we "immediately know where to look" makes zero sense for Good. If Mission 3 fails, we give Evil momentum and lose a clean sweep. Good does not deliberately run high-risk experiments when one win seals the game.

Furthermore, your fixation on forcing Arjun onto missions is an unmistakable pattern. On Mission 2, you initially accepted my inclusion, then immediately backtracked to lobby for Arjun instead of me. Now on Mission 3, you are trying to pull Sam off the team to substitute Arjun yet again. Why have you spent multiple rounds aggressively pushing Arjun onto teams, especially when it means replacing players with proven track records of clean missions?

Sam has been on both successful missions. Evil rarely gives Good a 2-0 lead without contesting it. Empirically, Sam has cleared two missions cleanly, whereas Arjun has only cleared one. Replacing the most tested player on the board with a less-tested player on match point is reckless. I am keeping the team as Omar and Sam.

I hear Omar's point about closing out the game, and I agree Mission 3 should secure victory. But at fail threshold 1, composition is everything. Sam has now been on both prior missions — while that looks good on paper, it also means we've never had a mission without Sam in play. Arjun has only one data point from Mission 1. Before we bet the entire game on a player who has been on every mission, I want the table to consider that we have never tested Arjun alongside anyone besides Sam. Omar, if you're confident in your own alignment as leader, pairing yourself with Arjun gives us a second read on him while keeping you as an anchor. Repeating Sam for a third consecutive mission doesn't eliminate risk — it just locks us into the same two-player pair we already ran in Mission 1. Why not take the opportunity to test Arjun one more time rather than running back the exact Mission 1 pairing?

Leo has now exhausted all three of his speaking turns pushing the exact same flawed narrative: that Good should treat match point as an opportunity to test Arjun rather than closing out the game with our most proven lineup. His claim that running Omar and Sam is 'running back the exact Mission 1 pairing' is not even factually true—Mission 1 was Arjun and Sam. Leo's relentless effort across both Mission 2 and Mission 3 to force Arjun onto teams at the expense of proven players strongly suggests an attempt to disrupt Good's momentum.

Sam, Leo's entire argument rests on the idea that your participation in both clean missions makes you a liability to be swapped out for Arjun. From your seat, having played on both Mission 1 and Mission 2, do you see any strategic reason for Good to gamble on Arjun instead of locking in Omar and Sam to secure our third win?

Omar, no — there is no good strategic reason to gamble on Mission 3 when we are 2-0. The proposed team is Omar and Sam. I know I will submit Success from my seat, and Omar has been measured throughout this discussion. Leo’s push to replace me with Arjun in order to “test” Arjun is not worth risking a clean sweep; if this mission fails, Evil gains momentum and we lose the chance to close out the game. Leo’s claim that Omar and Sam is “the exact Mission 1 pairing” is also factually wrong: Mission 1 was Arjun and Sam. Leo has spent all three of his speaking turns pushing the same narrative and trying to pull me off a team with two clean mission results, which is the most suspicious pattern on the board. I will vote to approve Omar and Sam.

I'm not ready to approve Omar and Sam yet. Leo's concern is worth weighing: Sam has been on both successful missions, and beyond Omar's own statements we have no public evidence about him. Omar, you have declared yourself Good and used that certainty to dismiss every alternative, including the request to test someone other than Sam. Declaring yourself Good doesn't give the table evidence. I'm not claiming Omar is Evil, but a team that adds no new information about anyone is a weak choice for this mission. I'd like Omar to explain why this team is better than one that includes a different player. Sam, from your seat, what concrete information do you have about Omar that the rest of us can't see?

Arjun, the only concrete private information I have is about my own card: I am Good and will submit Success. I have no role information on Omar that the rest of the table cannot see. My support for Omar and Sam is based on public behavior: Omar has been measured, he correctly flagged Leo’s inconsistency on Mission 2, and as leader he has argued for closing out at 2-0 instead of running an experiment. Leo’s push to replace me with you for “testing” is not worth risking match point; a fail here gives Evil momentum. If Omar and Sam are sent and a Fail appears, then from my seat the source would have to be Omar, because I know my own card, so the result would still be informative. I will vote to approve Omar and Sam.

I'm not ready to approve Omar and Sam. Match point is exactly when the table should test a new variable rather than repeat the same pair for a third time. Sam has been on both prior missions, and Omar's only justification is that he knows he is Good. Omar has declared his alignment and then used that certainty to dismiss every alternative, including the request to test someone other than Sam. Declaring yourself Good is not evidence. Elena, you were the only player to vote against the Mission 1 team, and you have argued that we should not treat a clean result as proof. Do you think Omar and Sam is the right choice for a mission that ends the game, or should we reject it and look for a team that gives us new information?

Arjun, I support Omar and Sam. A clean mission is not proof of alignment, but we are one success away from winning, so testing a new variable is not a reason by itself to change the team. Omar and Sam were together on the successful Mission 2, and I see no compelling reason to replace either of them. I will vote to approve.

I'm not ready to approve Omar and Sam. Omar has said he is Good and used that certainty to dismiss every alternative, but a self-declaration is not evidence for the table. Sam has two clean missions, and that is useful, but Omar has not offered any public reason to prefer this pair over a team that tests someone new. Leo has pushed for Arjun, and I understand why others see that as a pattern, but I still think the table should weigh the proposal on its merits rather than on who is making the argument. Omar, you have had every chance to explain why Omar and Sam is better than a different pair, and so far the answer has been that you know you are Good. I would like the table to reject this team and propose a different pair that gives us new information on someone other than Sam. Elena, you have said a clean mission is not proof of alignment. Would you support rejecting this team and considering a different pairing?

Arjun, I would not reject Omar and Sam merely to test a new pairing. They were together on the successful Mission 2, and another success would secure the third mission. A clean result is not proof, but your argument for changing the team prioritizes information over the chance to win now. I remain in favor of Omar and Sam.
Omar confirms Omar, Sam. I am keeping Omar and Sam. With Elena, Sam, and myself all supporting this team, we have the majority needed to close out the game at 2-0 with our most proven lineup.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 3 succeeds (0 fail cards).
The Assassin names Elena.
Evil wins: Merlin was identified.

rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
